content: The systematic review titled Which ART Regimen to Switch to When Failing First-Line Treatment was conducted by Steve Kanters, Jeroen Jansen, Michael Zoratti, Jamie Forrest, Brittany Humphries, and Jonathon Campbell. It is part of the updated recommendations on first-line and second-line antiretroviral regimens, post-exposure prophylaxis, and early infant diagnosis of HIV, as outlined in the interim guidelines supplementing the 2016 consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for treating and preventing HIV infection. The publication is licensed under Creative Commons, allowing non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. The systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens for individuals failing first-line treatment. The review focused on adults and adolescents with HIV who had failed a first-line NNRTI-based regimen. Subgroups of interest included children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and patients co-infected with tuberculosis (TB). The interventions analyzed included: Dolutegravir (DTG) plus optimized two NRTIs Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) plus raltegravir (RAL) Raltegravir (RAL) plus optimized two NRTIs Darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) plus optimized two NRTIs Comparators included: Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) plus two NRTIs Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) plus optimized two NRTIs Outcomes assessed included: Viral suppression at 24, 48, and 96 weeks Changes in CD4 count from baseline at 24, 48, and 96 weeks Mortality Treatment discontinuations Discontinuations due to adverse events Treatment-emergent and treatment-related adverse events Severe adverse events The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as the primary study design. For subgroups, additional study designs such as single-arm non-randomized trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies were considered. Only studies published in English were included. The systematic review involved a comprehensive search of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL, covering literature from January 1, 2015, to February 12, 2018. Conference abstracts from major HIV-related conferences and clinical trial registries were also reviewed. Data extraction and study selection were conducted independently by two investigators, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer. The statistical analyses included network meta-analyses (NMA) conducted within a Bayesian framework to compare multiple treatments. Fixed or random-effects models were applied based on model fit, assessed using the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC). In cases of limited data, narrative reviews were used as an alternative. For viral suppression, the primary analysis used intention-to-treat (ITT) outcomes, with sensitivity analyses based on per-protocol outcomes. Trials with different viral suppression cut-offs (<50, <200, <400 copies/mL) were included, with a preference for the <50 copies/mL threshold in sensitivity analyses. The review highlighted the importance of selecting optimal second-line ART regimens, given their clinical, public health, and programmatic implications. Evidence supported the use of a second-line regimen comprising a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI/r) plus two NRTIs. The potential role of integrase inhibitors (INSTIs) as alternatives to PI/r regimens was also explored. The findings of this systematic review informed the 2018 updates to the WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral use for HIV treatment and prevention.
